Jordan Fein’s production leans stylistically into the play’s strangeness but features terrifically naturalistic performances.

There is so much emotive power in Jordan Fein’s production, such extraordinary performances by Gelb and Chanda, and so many chilling parallels to current political indifference to the horrors around the world, that the play’s lack of internal coherence becomes irrelevant.
In a taut, timely and finely acted revival by American director Jordan Fein, a drama that might sound contrived and far-fetched becomes brilliantly gripping.
Broken Glass lacks the tight, exquisite structures of Miller’s best, the crackling charge of A View from the Bridge or Death of a Salesman, both revived here in recent years.

Brief interludes of plunging darkness and muggy, moody half-light only underscore the lack of privacy. A striking set from Rosanna Vize creates a narrow strip of pink-carpeted stage hemmed in closely by the audience on three sides.

At the Young Vic, the director throws everything at this late-period Arthur Miller play about a strange case of paralysis, set against the backdrop of Kristallnacht. Watching a fine cast go about their business over the course of two hours with no interval is like watching medics doing their best to keep a patient from slipping away.
This is not, until its closing moments, a subtle play.
The play is unable to hide its clumsy blending of medical paralysis, European persecution and American malaise.
But late works, including his 1994 play Broken Glass, now on at the Young Vic, can be a bit windy.

“We’re from Finland originally,” he unconvincingly maintains. Rosanna Vize’s set of a red carpeted thrust stage overlooked by clocks giving the time differences across the globe is an effective if somewhat puzzling design.
A new production of any Arthur Miller play is always a cause for great celebration, and this version of Broken Glass is no exception.
And it's worth it, because it is by Miller, to whom attention always should be paid, directed by Jordan Fein who gave us that remarkable Fiddler on the Roof, well cast and magnificently played
Broken Glass may refer to Kristallnacht, and the Jewish question, but it’s love, the fragility of humans and their relationships, that is at the heart of the matter.

Miller’s interrogation of antisemitism isn’t not relevant, it’s just that the political symbolism is overcomplicated by its entanglement with sexuality making it hard to detect what best to glean from Broken Glass.
This production of BROKEN GLASS however, is a far cry from Henry Goodman’s memorable 1994 turn at the National.
